question:
Patient note:
A 68-year-old retired civil engineer, accompanied by his spouse, came to the internal-medicine consult service at the request of urology for comprehensive medical clearance prior to a planned laparoscopic left partial nephrectomy; cross-sectional imaging obtained during evaluation of microscopic hematuria three weeks earlier had revealed a 2.4-cm enhancing cortical nodule at the lower pole of the left kidney with no regional lymphadenopathy, no vascular invasion, and no distant lesions on chest CT, and he has not yet undergone ablative therapy, systemic agents, or surgical intervention. He reports that the finding was completely unexpected, as he remains physically active—walking two miles every morning and tending a vegetable garden—and had no flank pain, gross hematuria, weight loss, night sweats, or bone discomfort. His medical background is otherwise remarkably limited: blood pressure has always been in the 120s/70s without pharmacologic help, lipid panel last month showed total cholesterol 174 mg/dL with LDL 88 mg/dL, and he has never been hospitalized except for an appendectomy in his twenties. He emphatically denies ever experiencing crushing substernal tightness, jaw or arm radiation, exertional diaphoresis, or emergency department visits for suspected coronary disease; he mows his own lawn without angina, has never undergone stress testing or cardiac catheterization, and an echocardiogram done two years ago to investigate a soft systolic murmur showed normal chamber sizes, preserved ejection fraction of 62 %, and no wall-motion abnormality. There has been no episode of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, ankle swelling, or diuretic use, and he walks up two flights of stairs carrying groceries without breathlessness. He also denies calf cramping with ambulation, non-healing ulcers, prior vascular bypass procedures, or ankle-brachial index measurements, and distal pulses have always been palpable and symmetric on routine physicals. He has never had sudden speech disturbance, unilateral weakness, facial droop, seizures, or transient monocular blindness, and a screening carotid duplex performed as part of a research study last year was unremarkable. Regarding pulmonary history, he quit a five-pack-year cigarette habit at age 30, has never carried an inhaler, does not cough chronically, and spirometry performed during a life-insurance exam five years ago showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.79 with normal lung volumes. A fasting glucose drawn during his yearly wellness visit two months ago was 108 mg/dL, and hemoglobin A1c measured 6.0 %; he follows a Mediterranean diet, has not been started on metformin or other hypoglycemic agents, tests his glucose only during community health fairs (all readings under 120 mg/dL), and denies polyuria, polydipsia, blurred vision, neuropathic symptoms, or prior episodes of ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar crisis. With respect to hepatology, a routine blood panel five years earlier showed mildly elevated alanine aminotransferase at 58 U/L; additional work-up revealed chronic hepatitis B surface antigen positivity with HBV DNA under 2,000 IU/mL, and ultrasonography plus vibration-controlled transient elastography have consistently demonstrated a smooth contour and stiffness readings in the 6–7 kPa range without splenomegaly or portal hypertension. He has never manifest jaundice, ascites, encephalopathy, or variceal bleeding; today’s laboratory chemistries show AST 42 U/L, ALT 64 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 82 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, albumin 4.3 g/dL, and INR 1.0, confirming preserved synthetic function despite the chronic viral infection. Serum creatinine this morning is 0.9 mg/dL (estimated glomerular filtration rate 92 mL/min/1.73 m²), blood urea nitrogen 13 mg/dL, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, calcium 9.1 mg/dL, hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.2 × 10⁹/L, and platelet count 212 × 10⁹/L. Urinalysis shows 3–5 red cells per high-power field, no protein, no casts, and negative nitrites. He tested negative for HIV at his last employment screening and has never noted swollen lymph nodes, fevers, or drenching sweats suggestive of hematologic disease. Current medications are limited to cholecalciferol 1,000 IU daily and an occasional ibuprofen 200 mg for post-gardening soreness; he takes no anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents, or supplements such as fish oil that might complicate surgery. Alcohol use is confined to a single craft beer on weekends, and he has never used illicit substances. Family history is notable only for a father who died of colon cancer at age 82; there is no premature cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease among first-degree relatives. Review of systems is otherwise negative for fever, chills, palpitations, syncope, cough, hemoptysis, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia, melena, easy bruising, dysuria, or rash. On examination he is well appearing, oriented, and conversant. Vital signs: temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 126/74 mm Hg seated in the right arm, heart rate 72 beats per minute regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air; body mass index is 26 kg/m². Cardiovascular inspection reveals no jugular venous distention; auscultation identifies a soft midsystolic ejection murmur grade 2/6 at the right upper sternal border without radiation or gallops. Lungs are clear with vesicular breath sounds bilaterally. Abdomen is flat and non-distended; liver edge is not palpable, there is no shifting dullness, and the kidneys are non-tender. No abdominal bruits are heard. Extremities are warm without edema; radial, femoral, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis pulses are 2+ and symmetric. Neurologic evaluation shows intact cranial nerves II–XII, normal strength and sensation in all four limbs, brisk deep tendon reflexes, and a steady heel-to-toe gait. Skin is free of telangiectasias, spider angiomata, or palmar erythema. Pre-operative electrocardiogram recorded in clinic displays normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats per minute with normal intervals, no pathologic Q waves, and no ST-T segment changes. The patient seeks guidance on peri-operative risk, vaccination for hepatitis B contacts, and long-term surveillance strategies for his newly identified renal mass in the context of otherwise excellent functional status, diet-controlled borderline glucose elevation, preserved renal function, and chronic but compensated viral liver infection.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) sums age and weighted comorbidity points:
- Age 68 (60–69 years) → 2.
- Localized solid tumor: counting the enhancing renal mass awaiting partial nephrectomy as a presumed renal malignancy, with no metastases → 2.
- Mild liver disease: chronic hepatitis B without portal hypertension or decompensation → 1.
- Other categories → 0. A1c 6.0% indicates prediabetes, not diabetes, and the renal mass does not itself imply renal insufficiency (creatinine 0.9 mg/dL).
Total = 2 + 2 + 1 = 5.
Final answer: 5
